overview.text: CPU cache memory is a small, high-speed store near the processor that keeps data and instructions a program may use again, helping avoid some slower trips to main memory. It matters because cached information can reach the processor more quickly, improving performance. Cache designs take advantage of locality: recently used information may be needed again soon, and nearby memory locations may be needed next. Many processors arrange caches in levels: L1 is typically closest, smallest, and fastest; L2 and L3 are generally larger and slower, though designs vary. A hit means the requested data is present; a miss sends the request onward, often to main memory. Caches commonly transfer data in blocks called cache lines.

key_facts.text: Three cache levels—L1, L2, and L3—are common, but some processors use a different arrangement. L1 is typically the smallest and fastest level, closest to the processor.
A cache hit occurs when requested information is already cached; a miss means the processor must request it from a slower level, such as main memory.
Caches exploit temporal locality (information used recently may be needed again) and spatial locality (nearby memory locations may be accessed soon).
Caches transfer data in blocks, often called cache lines, so a request for one location can bring nearby information into the cache too.
L1 caches commonly keep instructions and data in separate sections, because programs access them in different patterns.
